reviews.text: Super early days - I just finished level one and on to level 2 - but I just wanted to say this is (so far) completely playable on Steam Deck. It's not optimal (a mouse is super handy still!) but all controls work, including sticks to rotate and bumpers to zoom in and out. Loving the game so far, super relaxing, bloody gorgeous to look at, and all the dialog (so far) is super well done and perfectly silly. Big thumbs up and I can't wait to dig in more. I can't believe this is the standard of Early Access.. mind bogglingly polished!
Don't forget to open Kurzgesagt intro everytime before start game.

For what it looks like, I think it is taxing my hardware way too hard. Icons are enormous with no UI scaling option. Connecting pipes on spheres stayed enjoyable for about 30 minutes, and then it turned into a chore. This game lacks any challenge or adversary. It feels somewhat like a 3D remake of Mindustry. The logistical lines that are graphed out on the map are hard to read quickly, and are almost of no use. The game makes you accept quests constantly to complete them right afterward instead of making your currencies only a basic income. There is almost no benefit in optimizing your production lines. If it is set up, you can just speed up the game and win. There is a hint of challenge when you want to connect multiple production buildings to a receiving and a sending spaceport, but the game never forces you to explore these topological puzzles. In my opinion this is the most exciting aspect of the game, but it is not very rewarding, as you complete a stage anyway in 10 minutes, and all your setup factories don't matter anymore as their resources are not available across sectors.

I ended up getting a soft lock. Really though, even without that, its only 7 levels. Like 3-4 hours of game play. My rates about $1 per hour of entertaining game play, so a $4 game right now. WAY over priced.

[h1]成就和挑战设计的完全就是一坨屎，相互矛盾，恶意极大[/h1] [h2]就目前内容而言67不值得，但是未来可期。。。吗？[/h2] 先说优点：目前玩到星区6，有种戴森球计划/shapez+异形工厂+缺氧的既视感，小鸟动画做得很可爱，有种童年经营类手游的既视感。深空科技链作为导向结合小星球资源开采与太空航运和流水线排布设计做的不赖，游戏基本玩法已经大致摸清楚了。期待后续发挥，比如编辑界面拆除建造的灵活度，可以给建筑设计待机态等等。 为什么差评：成就设计与高星任务设计是一坨屎，连贯性太差甚至彼此矛盾。打个比方，在星区六的一个挑战中是把所有的冰封小行星的冰面全都溶解，那这个相当于是在上面全都放好融冰器就可以了，但冰封小行星一共有6颗，那这样的重复劳动对这种动脑子的游戏来说有何意义？ 假设我们达成了这个任务之后要去达成后两项任务——各项产品的产量星级评定，由于这个冰面是氧气和甲烷，如果我们把这个冰面全都溶解掉的话，相当于没有氧气来源和甲烷来源了，那在此之上建立的资源链和产业链会崩溃，更不要谈后面所有资源的产量达到三星级别完成全星收集。那意思就是我好不容易放满了的融冰器我还要再撤掉呗，或者说我还要重开一把，所以往往无法同时达成造成游玩体验坐牢。 并且开局引导节奏太慢,有很多次都是自己已经摸索到某个地方缺一个物品，此时需要把人物对话都点完才给物品，导致实际游戏卡手。而且引导也做得较差，自己玩下来发现有不少误区，而这些误区在一开始都没有引导得当。 当我们要去完成多星挑战的时候，往往都是两个小时之后了那也退不了款啊憋憋

Star Birds, developed by Toukana Interactive in collaboration with the science storytellers at Kurzgesagt – In a Nutshell, is a serene yet imaginative space-building and automation game that trades the gritty complexity of most factory simulators for something more peaceful, colorful, and quietly intelligent. At its core, it’s a game about managing a colony of birds—yes, birds—in space, harvesting resources from asteroids, constructing automated systems, and uncovering the mysteries of the cosmos. Despite the cuteness of its premise and visuals, there’s a lot of mechanical depth and design sophistication tucked beneath the surface, making it a welcome entry in the growing genre of cozy strategy games that aim to calm rather than overwhelm. From the moment the game begins, its tone is distinct and deliberate. Visually, Star Birds is a love letter to the Kurzgesagt art style, with its pastel color palette, clean lines, and precise geometry. Everything on screen feels friendly, inviting, and carefully designed. Unlike many space-themed games that lean into bleak or industrial aesthetics, Star Birds constructs a cosmos that’s more whimsical than hostile. Each asteroid you colonize is an intricate, procedurally generated playground where you’ll set up factories, logistics pipelines, and supply chains, all while rotating the asteroid in full 3D to maximize space. It’s a refreshing departure from the flat maps typical of the genre, forcing players to think in three dimensions and experiment with form-fitting layouts across curved surfaces. The gameplay revolves around exploration, construction, and optimization. You’re tasked with establishing colonies on asteroid fields, extracting materials, and automating production chains to generate increasingly complex resources. Your avian workers are at the center of everything, operating buildings and machinery with adorable precision. But this isn’t just a passive automation simulator; you have to plan carefully to avoid logistical problems, energy shortfalls, or inefficient layouts. The controls are intuitive, the interface is smooth, and there’s an understated satisfaction in watching a well-designed setup come to life as your bird colony thrives. Despite its relaxed pacing, the game does require attention and thoughtful planning, especially as more resource types and machinery become available. One of the most innovative aspects of Star Birds is its spatial design. Building around the full surface of rotating asteroids adds both complexity and novelty to the base-building genre. It’s no longer about maximizing horizontal space on a grid, but about mastering curved surfaces, managing pathing in three dimensions, and learning to orient your colony for optimal productivity. This rotational, spherical approach gives every asteroid its own challenges and character, and encourages creative thinking. It’s also visually compelling—watching your small network of machines and pipes gradually encircle an entire planetoid is oddly beautiful. The Early Access version of Star Birds already shows remarkable polish. Although not yet content-complete, the existing campaign offers structured goals, guided progression, and side missions that keep you motivated beyond the pure sandbox experience. Missions from quirky bird characters push you to adapt and expand, often rewarding exploration and experimentation. The procedural generation system keeps things fresh across multiple runs, while the mystery-laced storyline hints at larger discoveries in the universe, suggesting there’s more to this gentle cosmos than meets the eye. These narrative touches are minimal and non-intrusive, which is a smart decision—they enrich the world without bogging it down. While the game has received overwhelming praise, it’s important to understand what it is and what it isn’t. Star Birds is not trying to compete with high-complexity factory simulators like Factorio or Satisfactory. Its design is intentionally more accessible and meditative. There are no enemies, no survival mechanics, and no rush to optimize beyond what you find personally satisfying. That will be a major appeal to some and a drawback to others. For players looking for competitive play, deep tech trees, or late-game pressure systems, the current build may feel too relaxed or limited. Similarly, while the 3D construction offers a fresh take, it may not click with players who prefer grid-based layouts or who struggle with spatial reasoning on curved surfaces. That said, Star Birds is still in active development, and the Early Access model seems well-suited to its roadmap. The developers have been transparent about plans to expand systems, deepen automation mechanics, introduce more types of missions, and enrich the sandbox with rare materials, technological upgrades, and hidden secrets. With both Toukana and Kurzgesagt involved, there’s reason to be optimistic about the game’s future. The demo released during Steam Next Fest in mid-2025 was a breakout success, with tens of thousands of players praising its style, charm, and satisfying loop. It’s clear that a strong community is already forming around it, and the developers seem receptive to feedback. In the end, Star Birds is a rare game that manages to be calming without being shallow, and engaging without ever feeling aggressive. It encourages players to slow down, appreciate smart design, and enjoy the small wins—like perfecting a conveyor loop or discovering a new asteroid biome. It’s ideal for fans of base-building and management games who want something less stressful, more beautiful, and driven by a kind of quiet curiosity. Whether you're looking for a relaxing game to play at your own pace or a thoughtful experience that lets you unwind while still engaging your mind, Star Birds is already shaping up to be one of the more thoughtful and delightful entries in the genre. If its full release continues along the current trajectory, it may well become a modern classic of cozy strategy gaming. Rating: 9/10

I love automation/factory games. I love puzzle games. I love educational videos from those guys, yet this game... I just don't enjoy. With puzzle games you have to figure out *how* to solve a puzzle. In here that isn't as much of a challenge so it is a pretty shallow puzzle game. In factory games it is about efficiency and scaling. But in here the choices for what to mine and where to mine and how to process it are so limited that it really isn't a factory game. What is more in many cases due to routing limitations the more you are trying to scale the harder it gets (or even impossible). At the end it mostly feels like a tedious exercise of routing pipes that can't overlap (which I guess is the puzzle part), but this really isn't fun to me. If I was a dev I would keep asking myself a question: what is that at any point in time that the player is supposed to have fun doing and derive satisfaction from. Is that about overcoming routing limitations? Than there should be more tools to make it more of a gameplay. Is it about delivering more stuff faster? Than the game should probably get a rework in how asteroids work in the first place. What is more achievements (how many stars you get per level) seem fairly weird. Some of then just require you to keep building than undoing production lines so that you don't trigger "how many buildings of a type" you had. That is also a weird concept - why would I want to destroy my own stuff just to redo it, because the game limits the number of buildings I get to build? Or achievements about never upgrading. So that everything is just slower? Upgrades don't change anything fundamentally, they just make buildings basically faster. So how is that an achievement to play in a slow mode? It's just weird. I am puzzled by the amount of positive reviews. Yes the game is beautifully animated and colorful, but there's no good gameplay here at the moment. Maybe the problem is that you get a really talented team of animators, storytellers etc that worked so well for their YouTube videos, but what is missing is someone who designs gameplay.

I get what this game is trying to be, but resource gathering economy/factory sims need to be more wide and less tall. The game is played in levels with the objective to create some end goal item or resource, and you have to combine the resources on all the asteroids to get to it. That being said, it sort of plays more like a puzzle than an economy sim - what's the most efficient way to gather the bits and put them together in the fastest time? (Time to complete is huge points for score at the end of a level) I would rather see an economy sim where there's less of a solution to a problem and more of an exploration of building something or many things. Also, it's kind of a brain ache to rotate the asteroids to place structures. p.s. Kurzgesagt is awesome and good on you for giving video games a go.

If you’re under eight years old, or if this is your very first Factorio-style game, this might be a decent starting point. It does have its flaws, but since it’s still in Early Access, those issues are excusable for now. In fact, it may even be worth waiting a few more months before diving in. If you’re a fan of Kurzgesagt, giving it a try once isn’t a bad idea either. I’m a big fan myself—I’ve watched most of their YouTube videos more than three times—and in that sense, playing this feels more like an act of fandom than a pursuit of fun gameplay. The game may also appeal to those who enjoy puzzles and have an interest in space exploration. But outside of those categories, this isn’t likely to be a rewarding experience. I can’t help but feel that the creator’s intentions and the values this game is aiming for feel too old-fashioned for something that calls itself a “game.” Educational content made into a game is usually dull, and while this is perhaps the most entertaining of that bunch, it still feels like all the “addictive fun” elements have been deliberately stripped away. The mechanics aren’t particularly engaging, and the story doesn’t provide any real sense of immersion either. At best, it plays like a puzzle meant to introduce players to the idea of factory games. The system design itself feels awkward and somewhat flawed. It’s not the kind of game that encourages divergent thinking like city-building titles do. A city-builder can nurture creativity and planning skills, while also letting players fill in a blank canvas in their own way. Here, however, the rigid tech trees, strict procedures, and sector-optimized processes prevent that sense of freedom—and even mods or user maps wouldn’t meaningfully fix this. At the same time, it doesn’t really encourage convergent thinking either. While it could, in theory, teach some academic concepts, the connections between elements, parts, and item combinations are too loose to serve that purpose. On top of that, the pacing is slow, there’s no competition with others, and no skill-based challenges. Resources are infinite, space is generous, and time is abundant. The existing challenges mostly resemble repetitive problem-solving tasks that require steady effort rather than creativity or sharpness. Overall, it can feel relaxing to play at a leisurely pace, but unless you’re brand new to this genre, there isn’t much incentive to keep going. The low degree of freedom and lack of challenge make it hard to recommend. And while there might be ways to address both issues, it’s hard to see why this particular game would be the one worth investing in. The visuals are spectacular (they truly did bring their video style into 3D) but... The gameplay just isn't there at all. They tried to polish off the edges from the automation game genre (think baby's first Factorio, Satisfactory, or Dyson Sphere), but too much core material got thrown out with the bathwater. For one, level-based games are antithetical to automation games. Resetting your hard work to start level "3-4" or whatever just doesn't feel good, and the story (it's just some cute but paper-thin space bird chatter) isn't compelling enough to keep you going. Makes it feel like a phone app. But the real kicker is that they eliminated the idea of a progression tree (even Shapez has upgrades), because of course that wouldn't work in a level-based game. The tools you start with (and crucially: their limitations) are stuck that way for the rest of the game. Instead, progression is an endless carousel of new materials and crafting recipes (plus a few gimmick methods of mining for them). The result is that Star Birds plays like a different kind of game entirely. It's essentially like untying a knot repeatedly, or playing a simple kind of solitaire. Each new level has a limited number of asteroids, which have a limited number or spots for launch pads, and a limited number of each kind of mining spot, and a (very!) crammed space for placing buildings. There's no creativity or thought process in solving the problem of connecting everything together. It's faster, easier (and almost more fun because you can see it all more clearly) to just make a simple flowchart on a piece of paper and then close out the game because you already solved the level and it will be an enormous headache to try to place it all down and plug it all in. It's very telling that if cross-over pipes existed, the challenge from every level would be essentially non-existent. It's a waste of good material. Every hour they spent on the visuals and animations between levels (or the admittedly very satisfying pipe drawing system) is an hour that could've been spent on building fun new tools for advancing automation, or maybe some more interesting twists on the puzzle level format. Here's some free ideas: - A way to go over pipes. - Building platforms or capturing new asteroids. - A way to put pipes over your other pipes. - Recipes that limit others, so you have to balance rates instead of just building thoughtlessly. - Something that makes you go back and do an older level differently, maybe a resource is now toxic to others. - Some kind of way to make your pipes pass over the pipes you've already placed. - Material logistics, like storing, sorting, switchable pipe junctions. Maybe even some simple logic gates. - [b] Cross. Over. Pipes. [/b] For the love of god. If it's a puzzle game the levels should've been more like puzzles. If it's an automation game they should've played some other automation games first. If it weren't for the visuals this would be a 1/10 4/10

In its current state, I cannot recommend this game. I love the idea, the story and art is cute, but underneath that veneer is a big problem - space. By mission two and three, things are starting to compound and get chaotic. I get it - it's basically a factory sim game, just set in outer space on asteroids. Cool concept, its what made me buy the game. However, I started mission four and things got too chaotic, too quickly. Issues: - Not enough space (meaning asteroids are just way too small). I need more "dead space", I need more surface area on the asteroid OR I need more asteroids that are "throw away" asteroids. This wouldn't be as much of an issue if it weren't for the second problem.... - Pipelines. Pipelines cannot overlap or underlap. If they could cross-cross applesauce on top of each other, then space would not be much of an issue. As it is, though, you can only (at least, by mission 4) make a beeline direction. The game offers a hub so you can connect pipes to one hub, then split pipes out from that hub to go to other places - but this is basically useless as it doesn't address the core issue of pipes being unable to cross over/under each other. I understand them not going through, but other factory sim type games literally solve for this in the first 5 minutes. - I cant tell if I love or hate the tutorial. I think my issue is really with the UI, but I cant put my finger on it. It doesnt feel as smooth as it should, but at the same time, I cant tell/decide what might improve that or if it just needs a total overhaul. I will say, responsiveness to clicks in game - I want to move fast in this game and the game forcibly slows me down. As soon as a task is done, I want to click it to turn it in so I can begin the next one. Instead, the game forces me to wait as it "flips" the task over, indicating it's complete. - Lastly, a cardinal sin. There's a speed up button but it comes at the cost of technology points, which is a consumable resource. Granted, with a PROPER flow of the game, tech points shouldnt be a big bottleneck (or maybe a bottleneck at all for pro players) but for me, when I want to speed things up so I can farm up resources, it feels like a punishment to spend tech points. Other games do this for free. I cant understand the point behind making a requirement to pay it. This is not a bad game, per se, but it needs polish and in some cases a rework. If you're die hard fans of these types of games, feel free to consider buying it - but I would wait for a really good sale first. This is one of those games where it's sort of a 5/10. It's not great, but it's not awful. Don't let the art style and lo-fi music fool you though - this is NOT a cozy game. A charming factory concept that feels too simplistic and fiddly to truly shine. Star Birds is a factory-building game built around interplanetary logistics. The core idea is that you manage production chains across multiple planets and send resources back to HQ to unlock research and progress further. On paper, that’s a solid premise. In practice, however, the game feels overly simplistic and somewhat childish in tone and design. While the interplanetary logistics gimmick is interesting, the constant shuffling of materials between planets becomes more tedious than satisfying. Instead of feeling like a clever logistics challenge, it often feels fiddly and unnecessarily cumbersome. It’s clear that the game was made with care and affection, and there’s a certain charm to it. Unfortunately, the simplicity and pacing just didn’t click for me.

I love kurzgesagt, so it sucks to give this game a thumbs down. I hope by the time of the full release it will be a more polished experience. It just doesn't know what it wants to be yet. Is this a story oriented space explorer? A playable version of a kurzgesagt video? A tycoon logistics game? A mobile style puzzle game? The truth is that its trying to be all of these things at the same time and failing everywhere. The game advertizes itself like a satisfactory/factorio style experience, but wipes all of the work you did after an hour and makes you restart on a new level. I wanted to build a sprawling network of asteroids with different resources juggling along transit routes, but after an hour we packed up and moved on to a new system and restarted from scratch. I tried the freemode, but you need to complete dozens of levels to unlock the entire tech tree before playing or its just a bore without any challenge. I figured the story mode must therefore be the focus, and I'll enjoy a deep dive into astrophysics and space exploration, but in reality its just a text adventure with the kurzgesagt birds and a repetitive gameplay loop. The steam achievements show that im not alone in this feeling. Aside from the gameplay loop, there are some minor visual bugs when transitioning from map to planet sutfaces and back quickly. It is not all bad though, it just needs work. The art direction is incredible, and the gameplay itself when in a system is great. It has loads of potential, and I hope they can resolve this major design conflict before the full release.

A game that has an interesting twist. I can see Factorio and Mindustry in this to an extent but it is unique enough to have potential. I think personally the flow state of a lot of the game could be better. After 7 hours and exploring how far the progression will take you.... It's kind of a let down. The concept is great, the ingredients are there for a great game, however I feel it's missed it's mark. There is another comment that says the game doesn't know what it wants to be and I feel the same way. After an hour or 2 of grinding in a sector.. You have to move on without any of the hard work you just made. I feel personally that instead of using credits from repeatable side collection missions, you could use all the resources you've collected so far in the campaign as a bank. It would really make you want to build up the planets in advance before moving on. That way as you get further, things get more expensive and resources cost more. Something along those lines would make your previous sectors and asteroids feel more meaningful and worth putting the time into. Yeah you have the rewards but they don't help much for the campaign as they are more just achievement seeking. Make the buildings upgradable by resources, that is something else banking the resources could be used for. Need to make something produce more quickly or need to upgrade it to where you can bank more or even change the flow state of everything better, then allow buildings to be upgraded by resources. Just something that gives all previous work a purpose or reason. Because moving on to a new sector and wiping everything really killed it for me. Another thing I want to touch on, is being able to swap and route between the asteroids a bit better. I have to click out and hover over each of the asteroids and wait to see what resources I have leaving one asteroid and heading to another. I feel like if you set up a launch pad or a landing pad, you could direct it better. Something to indicate what I have coming off of one asteroid and want to redirect it to this one. Maybe a menu list of launchpads that are built and where they are heading. That way you can click to instantly redirect it to this landing pad instead of dragging it from 4 asteroids away across the sector. This game has potential. I recommend it for those who want to give it a chance. But there are things that can be improved. I think I'm going to put it down for a while and revisit it at a different time. But please go into this knowing that a lot of the time you put in, gets reset every level/sector of the campaign.

I found this game through Kurtzgezagt, whom I absolutely adore. Star Birds is vividly colorful and has the wonderful, familiar art style I expect, but as far as factory sims goes... There are better ones available out there. After Sector I, gameplay became complicated enough to get me concerned as to what later-gameplay will look like. At the end of Sector II, I was struggling to organize my productions in a way that didn't get me lost and result in me scanning through planets looking for the specific factory. And by the time I finished Sector III, I was exhausted and had a headache from the desperate attempts at ensuring my shipping lines weren't getting stopped up and indeed going to all the right places. For a game like this, it really needs a production and logistics view, where you can see all of your produced resources, which machines are making them and where, alongside the ability to re-configure resource launchpads remotely. This is the biggest reason I think I can't recommend this game as a factory sim; it's far, far too easy to get lost in my own productions, even if I take my time and build very carefully. Secondly, on-planet transport and power lines need to be able to cross over/under each other! This is such a big issue that makes organization even more difficult, because it means I have to run lines every which way in order to scale up production on one planet. Pass-over/under lines are a must-have for factory sims. As I primarily bought Star Birds to support my favorite YouTube group, I won't be refunding it, but fair warning: Don't expect Star Birds to feel streamlined or intuitive. 5/10. ;w;

Disclaimer: This is NOT a factory game. This is a master's course in Topological Graph Theory DISGUISED as a factory game. I find it prudent to compare a shared problem-solving experience many players will encounter throughout a myriad of factory games. This, of course, is what players do when confronted with a belt crossing. In Factorio, when you need to cross belts, the solution is simple: Build an underground belt that travels underneath the first. This is easy and intuitive to understand, and demonstrates how the best solution to a problem is often the simplest one. In Shapez 2, when confronted with the same problem, you can increase or decrease the machine layer to pass belts underneath or above one another. This, of course, mirrors the larger gimmick of the game: the freedom of layered building. In Satisfactory, there are perhaps a hundred different ways to solve this singular problem, each neither inferior nor superior to another. Rather, each is unique and different. You could simply build a conveyor lift to rise one conveyor over another. Or, if the look of lifts is displeasing to you, you could use a conveyor support to form a sloped conveyor, producing a more sleek and elegant design. If, however, neither of these seemed appealing, you could simply merge the two belts and use a smart splitter further down the line to re-separate them. For whatever reason. The point is, these many solutions to the singular problem of a belt crossing symbolize Satisfactory's core design principle: Each person's factory is unique to them, and no person's way of playing the game is superior to another's. Thus, we see a game's fundamental essence revealed in the solutions to this problem. So, you may ask, what fundamental essence does this game reveal of itself through this very same problem? Well, it is a simple, blunt response: TOO. GODDᾹMN. BAD. THERE IS NO EASTER BUNNY. THERE IS NO TOOTH FAIRY. AND THERE IS NO BELT CROSSING!!! In this game, your enemy is not the numbers. It is not the throughput of your belts, nor the availability of your resources. It is not logistics, it is not production, it is not scale. In this game, your enemy is none other than Mathematics herself. And she has risen scorned. 10/10 game, would recommend

Wow, just wow! I honestly don't think I've had this much fun with such a simple, charming game in a long time. First of all, I love Kurzgesagt and I think the game really captured not just their style visually and musically, but also the writing and overall fun the videos tend to have. I am very impressed with how well these translated to a video game. I also think the game itself is super fun, and I cannot wait to see it continue to be developed. There are very (VERY) few quirks here and there that show it's an Early Access game (like missing translations in the French version, or the camera moving when you are trying to just reach the bottom buttons), but the game DOES feel very polished, optimized, and honestly pretty done already. As of right now, the game stops at sector 14, which netted me about 22h of gameplay. That being said, I enjoyed every minute of it, and I can't wait for the next update. I highly recommend you try out the game, it's great fun, and even though it's currently in Early Access, it does feel far along enough to be already well worth the asking price.
